# Energy, Goodput, and the Physics of Frontier AI

Model quality narratives often ignore the industrial reality underneath: AI is becoming an energy-and-systems problem as much as an algorithms problem.

## Stranded energy → intelligence

Crusoe’s Chase Lochmiller describes a vertically integrated path from power to AI factories—energy generation, data centers at multiple scales, and managed AI cloud services. The strategic insight is geographic and thermodynamic: put compute where energy is stranded or cheap, and treat electrons as the feedstock of intelligence.

Amin Vahdat (Google) sharpens the systems metric that matters: not peak FLOPS, but **goodput**—delivered useful work after slowdowns, failures, and restarts. At 1,000–100,000 tightly synchronized accelerators, one failed component can stall a synchronous training or serving job. Checkpointing, restart, and network design dominate real economics.

## Scaling beyond “more GPUs”

Jensen Huang’s Dynamo framing emphasizes that AI crossed from impressive capability into *paid useful work*—agents people hire by the hour. That monetization justifies infrastructure spend, but also intensifies competition for power, packaging, networking, and software that keeps fleets utilized.

More speculative bets push the boundary further: Starcloud argues the cheapest long-run compute may be in space (energy and cooling physics), while Unconventional AI argues digital von Neumann substrates are the wrong physics for intelligence-per-watt (see companion article on substrate compute).

### Practice checklist

- Budget reliability and restart cost into training TCO, not only GPU sticker price
- Track goodput and utilization alongside model quality
- Site selection is an AI strategy decision: power, latency to users, and cooling
- Assume energy constraints arrive in years, not decades

# Enterprise AI Diffusion: Reinvention Beats Feature Packs

Enterprises asked for AI, then rejected much of what they got. Sequoia’s enterprise conversations—Aaron Levie (Box), Elias Torres (Agency), Block’s Goose agent, Crosby in legal—explain why: **diffusion is an org problem**, not a model-demo problem.

## What slows adoption

- Workflow mismatch: copilots that do not change systems of record
- Trust and permissions: agents without clear audit trails
- Unit economics: seats and token burn without outcome pricing
- Change management: managers buy tools; teams protect process

Aaron Levie’s “reinvent yourself in the AI age” framing treats AI as a chance to rebuild product assumptions (content, collaboration, agents over files), not to sprinkle chat widgets. Crosby’s “deal velocity, not billable hours” shows vertical AI winning when it optimizes a business metric incumbents under-serve.

## Practices that work

- Start from a measurable workflow KPI (cycle time, escape rate, recovery time)
- Give agents narrow production scopes with logs humans can correct
- Expect to rebuild internal platforms (IT, identity, eval harnesses)—Serval’s “rebuild IT for AI” theme
- Price for outcomes where possible; token passthrough rarely aligns incentives

articles.body:
# Own Your Weights: Why Companies Are Building Private Intelligence

Frontier APIs made it easy to ship AI features. They also created a trap: the more successfully you deploy AI, the more your COGS and dependency rise on someone else’s model. Across Sequoia’s recent conversations, a clear product doctrine is forming—**not your weights, not your product**.

## The problem with renting intelligence

Intelligence is becoming the product, not a feature bolted onto an app. If a single lab’s black-box model absorbs every customer’s data exhaust and taste, application companies become thin wrappers. Sonya Huang frames the alternative as *decentralized intelligence*: a solid open core, with each company building bespoke intelligence on its own data, workflow, and judgment.

Companies move toward owned models for four practical reasons:

1. **Cost** — Especially for low-margin businesses, API bills scale with success. Owning (or heavily specializing) weights is often the only durable unit-economics path.
2. **Speed** — In coding, security, and other latency-sensitive domains, a smaller custom model can beat a giant general model because tokens arrive faster.
3. **Performance** — Open and mid-size models can now outperform closed giants *on your domain* when post-trained well.
4. **Control** — Partnerships with labs can be excellent and still leave you wanting independent legs to stand on.

## What “owning intelligence” actually means

Fireworks CEO Lin Qiao’s framing is useful: ownership starts with **data**, not with GPUs. Public pretraining solved common tasks. Your company exists because it solves a *specific* task with specific taste. Owning intelligence means:

- Curating high-quality production data (and synthetic data that enriches it)
- Turning that data into weights via post-training techniques matched to the failure modes you see
- Keeping judgment and customer understanding inside the model loop, not only in prompt text

Post-training is how you “keep your taste.” An off-the-shelf API can imitate a category; it rarely encodes why *your* company should win.

## The new battleground is the intelligence layer

Application companies and foundation labs are racing toward the same user. The fight is no longer only UI and GTM—it is who shapes the intelligence users feel. That is why “applied research labs” inside product companies (Harvey, Factory, Glean, and peers) matter: evals, harnesses, and domain post-training are becoming core R&D, not side projects.

### Practice checklist

- Measure AI COGS as a first-class metric; treat rent-vs-own as a finance decision, not only an ML one
- Inventory tasks where latency, privacy, or domain jargon dominate—those are post-training candidates
- Build evals that encode taste before you fine-tune anything
- Prefer techniques that scale with *your* data and compute, not with more handcrafted prompts alone

# Three Quarters to AGI—and What Still Blocks the Last Mile

Demis Hassabis’s Sequoia conversation is notable for calibrated optimism: substantial progress toward AGI, with remaining gaps that are conceptual, not only “more scale.”

## What “mostly there” usually means in these talks

Across Hassabis, Silver, Sutton, and OpenAI/Anthropic builder talks, a shared picture emerges:

- World models and multimodality matter beyond text
- Reasoning and long-horizon agency are recent phase changes
- Continual learning / experience is still underdeveloped relative to static training
- Science and robotics remain harder than coding because data and verifiers are scarcer

Hassabis’s scientific agenda (and DeepMind peers on scientific AI) treats AGI less as a chatbot end-state and more as a system that can generate and test knowledge in the world.

## Builder takeaway

Do not plan products as if capabilities are frozen, and do not plan as if every domain is one fine-tune away. Prefer architectures that absorb new model generations, and domains where you can create experience loops and verifiers.

articles.title: RL Environments: The Missing Dataset for Real Work

# RL Environments: The Missing Dataset for Real Work

Reinforcement learning for agents is no longer only a lab technique. The bottleneck has shifted from “can we do RL?” to **can we build environments that look like the economy?**

## What an RL environment contains

Mercor’s Brendan Foody describes three parts:

1. **Worlds** — the docs, sheets, messages, and project state of real work
2. **Apps** — high-fidelity clones of tools people actually use (Salesforce, ServiceNow, M365…), reachable via MCP, CLI, or computer use
3. **Tasks** — prompts plus verifiers (rubrics, unit tests) usable for eval *or* training

Frontier labs cannot automate “everything on a laptop” without covering the distribution of worlds, apps, and tasks across jobs. That distribution is vast—think hundreds of labor categories, each with its own software stack—and humans remain central to constructing it, often with models in the loop.

## Why application companies should care

RL environments used to be lab infrastructure. Now they determine whether your agent learns *your* workflow or a generic demo. “GitHub for RL environments” style platforms (Prime Intellect and peers) point to a market for sharing, versioning, and composing environments—similar to how datasets and benchmarks standardized earlier ML eras.

If you only eval on chat rubrics, you will overfit to eloquence. If you train and eval in environments with verifiers, you can reinforce *completed work*.

## Constraints

- Building faithful app clones is expensive and legally delicate
- Verifiers are hard for fuzzy knowledge work; easier for code, forms, and structured ops
- Expert-hour supply (labeling, scenario design) is a scaling industry of its own

### Practice checklist

- Write verifiers before prompts whenever possible
- Prefer environment-based evals for agent releases
- Invest in a thin slice of *your* app world before buying generic agent benchmarks
- Track expert hours as a first-class training cost

# Robot Data Factories: Sensorizing Humans to Train Physical AI

Language models pretrain on the internet. Robotics has no equivalent corpus. Sequoia’s robotics conversations converge on a manufacturing problem: **how to produce experience at scale**.

## Sensorize the expert

Mecka’s Josh Gao focuses on capturing human demonstration with rich sensing—turning people into data factories for robot policies. The scarcity is not motor hardware alone; it is high-quality, diverse, task-complete trajectories in the real world. Science-fiction metaphors aside, the engineering thesis is prosaic: instrument humans, warehouse the multimodal data, train generalists.

Physical Intelligence and NVIDIA’s Jim Fan push the complementary “end game”: general robots that can be prompted into many tasks, with foundation models for the physical world. Hugging Face’s Thomas Wolf discusses distribution—“app store” dynamics—for robot skills once a platform exists.

## Constraints unique to physical AI

- No internet-scale pretraining dump; every hour is expensive
- Embodiment gap: sim-to-real still bites
- Safety incidents have physical consequences (Zipline’s zero-incident ops culture is a related lesson in autonomous systems)
- Data rights and workplace instrumentation are socially fraught

### Practice checklist

- Design data capture before robot SKUs
- Prefer tasks with clear success criteria for learning signal
- Budget for continuous data ops, not one-off demos
- Separate fleet reliability engineering from model research early

# Intelligence Per Watt: Rethinking the Computing Substrate

Most AI efficiency work optimizes algorithms or GPU kernels. Naveen Rao (Unconventional AI) argues the deeper limit is the **physical substrate** of computation—and that brains are an existence proof we are ignoring.

## The energy wall

Humanity’s brains use ~20W each (~160GW total). Global electrical capacity is thousands of gigawatts, but AI training/inference is racing toward a world where energy—not ideas—is the binding constraint within a few years. Digital accelerators improved cost and packaging faster than true energy-per-useful-operation with memory traffic.

Brains (and even small animals) achieve complex behavior at milliwatts. That gap is not a rounding error; Rao estimates orders of magnitude between current digital practice, lithography limits, biology, and thermodynamic bounds (Landauer).

## Non-von Neumann dynamics

The proposed direction: trainable coupled oscillators / nonlinear dynamical systems where physics *is* the compute—state and function overlap, rather than endlessly shuttling tensors between memory and ALU. Training becomes steering trajectories in state space. The claim is not that GPUs stop mattering tomorrow, but that ASI-level abundance requires a different computing abstraction than 1940s digital floating-point machines designed for other workloads.

Startup advantage, in his telling, is lack of baggage: months-to-tapeout cycles versus incumbent chip roadmaps.

### Why builders should care now

Even if you never fabricate oscillators, the framing changes product and infra planning: energy per task becomes a first-class KPI; “just buy more GPUs” eventually collides with grid reality; co-design between models and machines will intensify.

### Sources

# Building a Web That Agents Can Use

The public web was built for human eyes and ad clickers. Agents need machine-reliable retrieval, tools, and permissions. Parallel’s Parag Agrawal argues for a **new web layer for AI agents**—infrastructure that makes the internet legible and actionable for non-human browsers.

## Why the old web breaks

Classic search and scraping assume a human in the loop to disambiguate layout, CAPTCHAs, and junk. Agents operating at volume need structured access patterns, freshness guarantees, and APIs that do not silently change. Otherwise every agent company reinvents brittle scrapers.

## Product implications

- Treat “agent traffic” as a first-class user persona in your SaaS (stable APIs, clear auth, machine-readable docs)
- Separately, agent platforms need retrieval substrates beyond ten blue links—corpora, browsers, and tool marketplaces
- SEO evolves into agent-led growth: Profound and peers explore ranking/visibility when the “reader” is an agent intermediary

The winners may be companies that make the web programmable for agents without turning it into a closed garden.
